The next meeting is set for the first Tuesday in January, with an open forum to follow the town manager's budget and five-year plan presentation.

why_it_matters: Licenses decide which businesses may legally serve food, sell alcohol or run entertainment in town, and the Simon-Pure letter means that business must go back before the board to keep operating.

A possible change to the jukebox requirement and fee could alter what local bars and restaurants pay, and residents will have a chance to comment on the town manager's budget and five-year plan at the planned open forum.

what_happened.line: The Select Board adopted a single tax rate for all classes for FY2020, pending state Department of Revenue approval; the vote was unanimous.
The board accepted the solar PILOT agreement for 190 Electric Avenue in final form, with one abstention, after comparing it with a depreciation model.
The board compared ten years of depreciation payments with twenty years of PILOT payments and heard that the PILOT yields more over time.
A motion on the common victualler license for a gas station and market at 400 Electric Avenue was made, but the recording does not make the outcome audible.
The board accepted the social media policy with the change to "town manager", and agreed to hold a public question session after the January budget presentation.

why_it_matters: A single tax rate means homes and businesses are taxed at the same rate per thousand dollars of value, so the commercial and industrial classes do not carry a higher rate than residential property.
The PILOT sets fixed payments from a solar facility over twenty years in place of taxes on its equipment as it depreciates, which changes how much that property contributes to the tax base.
The January budget presentation and the planned public question session are where residents can ask about FY21 spending before the budget goes to Town Meeting.
watch_next: December 3rd workshop on the old primary school, which is also to take up the public comment policy; no meeting Thanksgiving week.
The date of the public question session after the town manager's January budget presentation, to be set by the chair and town manager.

what_happened.line: The board found the dog dangerous, 4-0 with one abstention, and continued the hearing to October 15 at 7:30 for the penalty.
Testimony in the dog hearing is closed; the final penalty determination comes on October 15.
The board approved removal of the eight public trees Unitil recommended, and approved removing brush three inches or less, 4-1.
The board appointed citizen members to the TC Passios building design committee and ratified the principal clerk appointment.
The board recommended the Saliba property acquisition article, 4-0 with one abstention, and deferred its recommendation on the Butterfly Lane article.

why_it_matters: The Saliba purchase would be authorized in full and carried until state grants reimburse it, with the remainder borrowed, so it may affect future debt payments paid mostly from taxes.
The dog penalty is still undecided, and the tree and brush decisions touch roadside trees and scenic roads, with five trees the planning board did not approve still unsettled.
watch_next: October 15 at 7:30: the board's final penalty determination in the dangerous dog hearing.
The special town meeting vote on the warrant articles, including Saliba, and the board's deferred recommendation on the Butterfly Lane article.

meetings.headline: Select Board appointed members to Planning Board and Housing Authority and ratified three town hires; TC Passios committee interviews held.
meetings.summary: The board held joint meetings to fill vacancies on the Planning Board and Housing Authority, granted a one-day beer and wine license, and interviewed four candidates for the TC Passios building design committee. It ratified a Council on Aging van driver, a recreation director and an assistant town manager/HR director. The town manager reported on grants, the 925 Mass Ave search warrant and the draft special town meeting warrant, including a non-binding question on demolishing the old primary school. A resident objected to the three-minute public comment rule.

what_happened.line: The Select Board discussed with consultants which projects to bundle into a Complete Streets funding application, and the captions record no decision.
Members split over adding the Whalum area project and dropping item eight; the chair polled members one by one and the captions end before an outcome.
Dropping item eight and keeping items one, three and four would bring the request under the amount available, as heard.
A member asked why the town share differs for one project; the answer was that paving and drainage are not grant-eligible but count toward total project value.

why_it_matters: Which streets are in the application decides which sidewalk, crossing and road projects can draw state Complete Streets money instead of relying only on the town budget, mostly taxes.
Costs the grant does not cover, such as paving and drainage, stay with the town, so the mix of projects shapes the local share.

meetings.summary: The Select Board, joined by the Sewer Commission for appointments, ratified a new assistant treasurer and building commissioner, then handled a long agenda. what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 3-1, with one abstention, to let the Lake Shirley Improvement Corporation's notice of intent go to the Conservation Commission.
The board renewed PJ Keating earth removal permits 15, 16, 17, 27, 30 and 57, some by split votes with abstentions and with conditions attached.
The board accepted closure of permits 19 and 56 and the Lunenburg Water District permit, and did not renew them.
The board accepted the Open Meeting Law response with the remedial action paragraph replaced by a public comment sentence.
The board approved stop sign locations as submitted, and sent the old primary school repair question to the September 17 workshop.

why_it_matters: Earth removal permit renewals and the Lake Shirley notice of intent decide what excavation and lake work can go ahead, and the Conservation Commission review is where abutters can comment.

Repairs to the old primary school and any independent Lake Shirley water testing would be paid from the town budget, mostly taxes, so the workshop discussion is where those costs would first be weighed.
watch_next: The September 17 workshop, where the old primary school repairs will be taken up with the preservation commission invited.
The special town meeting set for November 12, 2019, with the warrant opening September 10 and closing September 30 at 5:00 p.m.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to renew all active earth removal permits for two weeks, until September 3, 2019.
The board announced the Conservation Commission chair will give a public apology at the next televised meeting and attend open meeting law training.
The finance director reported fourth-quarter FY19 collections slightly over estimates, and members debated estimating local receipts closer to actuals.
The finance director is to provide a ten-year history of local receipts against estimates, and the town manager is to ask about reviving the ad-hoc budget committee.
The board heard an informational solar PILOT draft for 190 Electric Avenue, and left the town manager evaluation process without resolution.

why_it_matters: Local receipts estimates set how much revenue the town counts on before the tax rate is set, so estimating closer to actuals would change how much is left over as free cash.
A solar PILOT is a fixed payment in place of ordinary property tax on a site, so its terms decide what that property contributes to the tax base over twenty years.
A revived budget committee would change how the Finance Committee, School Committee and Select Board coordinate before Town Meeting votes.
watch_next: The earth removal permits run only until September 3, 2019, so the board must act again by that date.
The ten-year local receipts history from the finance director and the chair's draft town manager evaluation policy are due back to the board.

what_happened.line: The Select Board accepted the draft assistant town manager/HR director position description, with one member opposed, so the town manager can advertise the job.
The board held a workshop on a special event license policy and agreed draft changes, including a license rather than a permit, a 100-person trigger and 200-foot abutter notice.

Lake Shirley residents used public comment to press the board on weed and algae treatment and an extension of the order of conditions needed to treat this summer.
The town manager reported on a state earmark, a recycling grant, MS4 engineering services and vacancies.

why_it_matters: The new assistant town manager/HR director position adds a salaried town staff post, paid from the town budget, mostly taxes, and the pay grade set now shapes that cost.
The special event rules would decide when organizers need a license and pay for advertising and abutter notice, which touches neighbors of events and anyone who holds one.
Whether Lake Shirley is treated this summer depends on an order of conditions extension, which bears on lake use and on association dues that fund treatment.
watch_next: August 6 Select Board meeting: the special event license policy returns, and a workshop on remaining policies is planned.
The extension of the Lake Shirley order of conditions, which the chair said would be taken up at a meeting the next day.

It approved a Unitil pole location and a one-day wine and malt license, and debated special event permit guidelines until the motion was withdrawn and a July workshop was proposed. It voted to invite talent bank applicants into reappointments, ratified seasonal beach appointments, released old executive session minutes, and went into executive session on litigation.

what_happened.line: The Select Board withdrew a motion to adopt special event permit guidelines and will rework the definition for a July workshop.
Lake Shirley residents spent long public comment on a dispute with the Conservation Commission over an order of conditions and an alleged conflict of interest.
The board approved a Unitil pole location on Pine Grove Road, with one member voting no, and a one-day wine and malt license for June 8.
The board voted to invite talent bank applicants to interview in the Conservation Commission reappointment process.
The board released listed executive session minutes, then went into executive session on litigation by roll call vote.

why_it_matters: Special event rules decide what events, such as those on Holman Street, may be held and what notice abutters get, and the definition is still unsettled.
Conservation Commission seats and orders of conditions affect lakefront owners, and the reappointment interviews change how residents can apply for those seats.

A state earmark for the Eagle House senior center, to be reimbursed against expenses by June 30, will affect free cash, and higher supply rates for electricity and gas from December 1 touch the FY20 budget.
watch_next: The July workshop on the special event permit definition, with the date still to be set with the town manager.
The June 11 workshop to set board and town manager goals, and the June 18 agenda with the July and August meeting schedule.

The board set a goal-setting workshop for June 11, with goals to be finalized June 18.
Members agreed the reappointment process goes on the June 4 agenda, with reappointments likely June 18 under a light-touch process.
The board voted on Finance Committee appointing-committee and MPO representative seats, and agreed to put labor counsel and a possible new meeting location on future agendas.
The board heard that the town's MS4 stormwater compliance plan involves engineering consulting over five years, and that a stormwater utility fee was discussed.

why_it_matters: A stormwater utility fee, if pursued, would be a new charge on property owners, and pay-as-you-throw bag fees are also due back before the board in June.
The electrical system at the TC Passios building is past its lifespan, so an upgrade is likely to need funding, probably through the town budget, which is mostly taxes.

what_happened.line: The Select Board split 2-2 on tabling the town manager's evaluation, then 2-2 on reading it tonight and discussing it next week; both motions failed.
The chair read the full composite evaluation into the record, and the board agreed to seek a consensus next week, with edits going to the chair meanwhile.
The board approved a toll booth, a cruise night road closure and an appointment to the Agricultural Commission; two other appointment votes were not audible.
The board approved an entertainment license for a three-day family event, amended to cap amplified music at eight hours a day.
The quarterly financial report was held over to next week and is to go first on the agenda; the missing ballot questions were left to the new board.

why_it_matters: The town manager's evaluation is the board's main review of who runs town departments, and its final form will not be set until the board meets again.
Ballot questions that did not reach the Town Meeting ballot will not be addressed until after the election, so voters should not expect them on this cycle's ballot.
The quarterly financial report, which shows how the current budget is tracking, was delayed by a week.

Whether the board endorses the town manager's recycling contamination grant application.

what_happened.line: The Select Board split 2-2 on the FY20 budget article, so it made no recommendation to Town Meeting on the budget.
The board recommended approval of article 23, the Brooks House building sale; the outcome of the vote on the land conveyance, article 22, was not audible.
The board was also deadlocked on article 21, the old primary school, and made no recommendation on it.
The board adopted a reimbursement policy with edits and approved abating an old ambulance receivable that had no supporting records.
After a long hearing on a draft special event permit policy, the board agreed to a 48-hour cleanup period; no final adoption is recorded.

why_it_matters: Residents at Annual Town Meeting will vote on the FY20 budget and the old primary school without a Select Board recommendation, so the floor vote carries more weight.

The special event policy, which sets rules for overnight camping, event limits and cleanup, is still a draft, and residents raised concerns about how it relates to a citizen petition bylaw on the warrant.
watch_next: Select Board meeting April 16, and an abutters workshop the week of April 30; there is no meeting April 23.
An 8 a.m. Select Board meeting on the morning of Town Meeting, when the remaining articles (4, 5, 6, 8, 24, 33 and citizen petitions) were deferred to the floor.

what_happened.line: The board voted 2-1 to add a sixth marijuana question, on prohibiting marijuana researchers, to the May election ballot.
The board added a warrant article for a local option excise on retail marijuana; the minutes record the vote as not audible.
The board extended the closing of the annual Town Meeting warrant to March 25 at 4:00 p.m., and tabled a two-night Town Meeting question to March 5 with public input.
A workshop on reusing TC Passios and conveying the old primary school and Brooks house drew public comment on offices, green space and leasing rather than selling.
The board will submit its senator funding list with fuel tanks at lowest priority, to be revisited in March.

why_it_matters: The marijuana ballot question and excise article put a local tax and a local rule before voters in May and at Town Meeting.
What happens to TC Passios, the old primary school and the Brooks house sets where town offices go and whether town land is leased or sold, which bears on a possible large building cost to taxpayers.
Whether Town Meeting runs one night or two decides when residents can attend and vote on the budget and warrant articles.

March 25 at 4:00 p.m.: the annual Town Meeting warrant closes.

The board will seek a Town Meeting article to fund detailed drawings of the TC Passios plan of record and will continue workshops with other groups.

why_it_matters: The old primary school and Brooks House are town-owned buildings, and any decision to repair, sell, lease or demolish them would come to Town Meeting as a funding vote and affect the town budget, mostly taxes.

Repair costs for the old primary school were described as near the cost of demolition, and the debt discussion shows these projects would compete with other building needs such as TC Passios, so residents may be asked to vote on drawings funding in May.
